title: Conditions of the Abdominal Cavity: Ascites, Peritonitis, and Adhesions
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers three disorders of the peritoneal cavity: fluid accumulation (ascites), infection (peritonitis), and scarring (adhesions). Ascites in cirrhosis is explained through Starling forces in the hepatic sinusoids and renal sodium retention driven by splanchnic vasodilation, and the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is read as a measure of portal pressure. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is contrasted with secondary peritonitis by source, organisms, fluid findings, and examination. Adhesions are explained as failed peritoneal fibrinolysis, leading to small bowel obstruction. Board questions usually give paracentesis numbers or an abdominal examination and ask for the mechanism or the cause.
prerequisites: Starling forces across capillaries and the role of lymph flow (Guyton and Hall)
Hepatic sinusoid structure, the space of Disse, and portal venous anatomy (GI-2, GI-5)
Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, ADH, and baroreceptor control of sodium balance
Peritoneum, peritoneal spaces, and visceral versus parietal innervation (GI-4)
Coagulation and fibrinolysis: fibrin, plasminogen, tPA, and PAI-1

connections.how: Cirrhosis supplies the sinusoidal portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation that cause ascites, and the same circulation leads to hepatorenal syndrome.

connections.to: The gut in the body cavities (GI-4)
connections.how: Peritoneal recesses determine where ascites, pus, and blood collect, and parietal somatic innervation explains localized pain and guarding.
Adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction in adults who have had abdominal surgery.
Enterobacteriaceae cause spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, while Bacteroides fragilis and other anaerobes mark secondary peritonitis and abscess.
Right heart failure also raises sinusoidal pressure and gives high-SAAG ascites, and effective arterial underfilling activates the same neurohormonal response as in heart failure.

Wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure, an estimate of sinusoidal pressure relative to the systemic veins.
The portion of blood volume that fills the arterial tree and is sensed by baroreceptors, which can be low even when total body fluid is high.

Infection of preexisting ascites with no intra-abdominal surgical source, defined by ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more.
Peritoneal infection from a breach or inflamed focus in an abdominal organ, such as a perforated ulcer or ruptured appendix.
Passage of gut bacteria or their products across the intestinal wall to mesenteric lymph nodes and beyond.
An abnormal fibrous band joining peritoneal surfaces that are normally separate.
The main inhibitor of tissue plasminogen activator; its rise after peritoneal injury allows fibrin to persist.
Obstruction of a bowel segment at two points, so the trapped loop cannot decompress and strangulates quickly.
Loss of blood supply to an obstructed bowel segment, leading to ischemia, necrosis, and perforation.

sections.title: Ascites in cirrhosis and the serum-ascites albumin gradient

blocks.text: Ascites forms when filtration into the peritoneal space outpaces lymphatic return. In cirrhosis, local Starling forces push fluid out of the liver and gut, and the kidneys keep retaining sodium and water that refill the leak.
Sinusoidal hypertension and the leak

Fibrous septa, regenerative nodules, and contracting activated stellate cells raise intrahepatic resistance. Portal hypertension is an HVPG above 5 mmHg and becomes clinically significant at about 10 mmHg or more. Sinusoids are fenestrated and leaky, so raised sinusoidal pressure drives fluid into the space of Disse and greatly increases hepatic lymph formation. When hepatic lymph flow exceeds what the thoracic duct can return, fluid weeps from the liver capsule and splanchnic capillaries into the peritoneum. The pressure must be sinusoidal: prehepatic portal vein thrombosis rarely causes ascites, whereas cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and right heart failure all do. Hypoalbuminemia from reduced hepatocyte synthesis lowers plasma oncotic pressure and adds to the leak but is not the primary cause.
Splanchnic vasodilation and renal sodium retention

Portal hypertension and translocated bacterial products increase splanchnic nitric oxide and other vasodilators, so splanchnic arterioles dilate. Systemic vascular resistance and arterial pressure fall, and baroreceptors sense a low effective arterial blood volume even though total body water and sodium are increased. As after hemorrhage, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone, and sympathetic tone rise, and ADH is released without an osmotic stimulus. Urine sodium becomes very low, ADH causes dilutional hyponatremia, and the retained fluid leaks out as ascites. Extreme renal vasoconstriction in the same setting produces hepatorenal syndrome (GI-13-C).

blocks.title: How cirrhosis produces ascites
steps: Fibrosis and nodules raise sinusoidal resistance
Sinusoidal and portal pressure rise
Splanchnic nitric oxide dilates arterioles
Low effective arterial volume sensed by baroreceptors
RAAS, sympathetic tone, and nonosmotic ADH rise
Kidneys retain sodium and water
Sinusoidal pressure and low albumin push fluid out; lymph overwhelmed
blocks.caption: Starling forces create the leak; renal sodium retention refills it.

blocks.text: Reading the fluid

The SAAG is serum albumin minus ascitic albumin, measured the same day. At equilibrium the oncotic difference across the barrier balances the hydrostatic difference, so a large gradient means high portal pressure. A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more indicates portal hypertension with about 97% accuracy. Ascitic total protein then separates the causes. In cirrhosis, collagen deposition in the space of Disse and loss of fenestrae (capillarization) make sinusoids less permeable, so fluid is protein poor (under 2.5 g/dL). In heart failure and early Budd-Chiari syndrome the sinusoids are normal, so fluid is protein rich (2.5 g/dL or more). Shifting dullness usually needs about 1,500 mL of fluid to detect.

blocks.title: SAAG and ascitic total protein
rows: Right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, early Budd-Chiari syndrome
Peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, pancreatic ascites
blocks.caption: SAAG shows whether portal pressure is high; total protein shows how much protein the leaking surface lets through.

blocks.title: Worked example: two high-SAAG fluids
blocks.text: Patient A: serum albumin 2.6 g/dL, ascitic albumin 0.8 g/dL, ascitic total protein 1.2 g/dL. Patient B: serum albumin 3.6 g/dL, ascitic albumin 1.9 g/dL, total protein 3.4 g/dL. Step 1: SAAG is 1.8 g/dL for A and 1.7 g/dL for B, so both have portal hypertension. Step 2: A has protein-poor fluid from capillarized sinusoids, which fits cirrhosis; protein under 1.5 g/dL also raises SBP risk (C02). Step 3: B has protein-rich fluid from intact sinusoids, which fits right heart failure or Budd-Chiari syndrome.

blocks.predict: Portal vein thrombosis with a normal liver causes varices. Will marked ascites develop?
blocks.explain: Usually not. The block is presinusoidal, so sinusoidal pressure and hepatic lymph formation stay near normal.

sections.title: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis versus secondary peritonitis

blocks.text: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, usually from infection, and the key distinction is the route. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a form of primary peritonitis, is infection of preexisting ascites with no hole or abscess in the gut. Secondary peritonitis follows spillage from, or spread of inflammation through, the wall of an abdominal organ.
How SBP develops

Cirrhosis weakens every barrier between gut bacteria and ascites. Slow transit allows bacterial overgrowth, portal hypertension makes the mucosa leaky, and enteric bacteria translocate to mesenteric lymph nodes and then into the blood. Portosystemic shunting lets portal blood bypass Kupffer cells, the liver's main bacterial filter, so bacteremia persists and seeds the ascites. Ascitic fluid contains little complement and opsonin, especially when total protein is under about 1.5 g/dL, so bacteria are poorly phagocytosed. Translocation favors aerobic gram-negative rods, so SBP is usually monomicrobial: Escherichia coli most often, then Klebsiella pneumoniae, and less often streptococci or enterococci. Anaerobes point to a perforation.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
steps: Bacterial overgrowth and leaky mucosa in portal hypertension
Gram-negative rods reach mesenteric lymph nodes
Shunted portal blood bypasses Kupffer cells
Bacteremia seeds low-protein ascites
Low complement and opsonins impair killing
Ascitic neutrophils reach 250/mm3 or more
blocks.caption: Barrier failure, hepatic bypass, and weak opsonization combine.

blocks.text: Ascites separates the visceral and parietal peritoneum and dilutes the inflammatory exudate, so SBP often produces fever, mild diffuse tenderness, worsening encephalopathy, or rising creatinine instead of a rigid abdomen, and some patients have no abdominal signs. Neutrophils arrive before cultures turn positive, so an ascitic neutrophil count of 250/mm3 or more establishes the diagnosis. In bloody fluid, about 1 neutrophil is subtracted for every 250 red cells. SBP cytokines worsen splanchnic vasodilation and can precipitate hepatorenal syndrome. In children, primary peritonitis classically complicates nephrotic ascites, often with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Secondary peritonitis

A perforated peptic ulcer, ruptured appendix, perforated diverticulum, infarcted bowel, or leaking anastomosis releases mixed flora: enteric gram-negative rods together with anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis, plus enterococci. The B. fragilis capsule promotes abscess formation. The parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves (T7 to L1 anteriorly, the phrenic nerve under the central diaphragm), so its inflammation causes sharp, localized pain, reflex guarding, and a rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness. Paralytic ileus, fluid shifts into the peritoneum and bowel wall, hypovolemia, and sepsis follow. A perforated viscus releases free air under the diaphragm on an upright radiograph.

blocks.title: Spontaneous versus secondary peritonitis
rows: One, usually E. coli or Klebsiella
Low protein; usually fails the criteria at right
Two or more: protein above 1 g/dL, glucose under 50 mg/dL, LDH above serum upper limit
Free air if a viscus perforated
blocks.caption: The chemistry criteria flag secondary peritonitis arising within cirrhotic ascites.

blocks.title: Worked example: infected ascites, but which kind
blocks.text: A man with cirrhosis has fever of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). Ascitic fluid: neutrophils 3,900/mm3, total protein 2.4 g/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL, LDH above the serum upper limit; Gram stain shows several organism types. Step 1: neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more confirm infected ascites. Step 2: protein exceeds 1 g/dL, bacteria and neutrophils consumed glucose, and cell breakdown raised LDH, so all three criteria are met. Step 3: with mixed organisms, this is secondary peritonitis from a perforation, not SBP.

blocks.predict: Why can SBP lack guarding when a perforated ulcer causes rigidity?
blocks.explain: In SBP, ascites dilutes the exudate and separates the layers, so parietal irritation is mild. Spilled acid and bowel flora intensely inflame the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, causing reflex spasm.

sections.title: Peritoneal adhesions and small bowel obstruction

blocks.text: The peritoneum is a single layer of mesothelial cells on a basement membrane over loose connective tissue. Its surfaces glide because they are smooth and lubricated, and it heals unusually well: after injury, mesothelium regenerates across the whole raw area at once from surrounding and underlying cells, so a large defect heals as fast as a small one, within about a week.
Why fibrin becomes scar

Any injury (surgical handling, drying, cautery, sutures that leave tissue ischemic, foreign material, blood, infection, radiation, or endometriosis) triggers inflammation within hours. Vascular permeability rises and a fibrin-rich exudate coats the damaged surfaces and glues neighboring ones together. Whether this glue dissolves depends on fibrinolysis. Healthy mesothelium releases tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which converts plasminogen to plasmin, and plasmin normally clears the fibrin within about 3 days. Injury and especially ischemia reduce tPA, while inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, TGF-beta) raise PAI-1. Fibrin then persists, and fibroblasts, macrophages, and new capillaries invade it. TGF-beta drives collagen deposition, and the fibrin bridge matures into a vascular fibrous band, sometimes containing nerve fibers. Most people develop adhesions after laparotomy, and peritonitis causes dense ones because infection and ischemia suppress fibrinolysis most strongly.

blocks.title: From peritoneal injury to adhesion
steps: Surgery, infection, or blood injures mesothelium
Fibrin-rich exudate bridges adjacent surfaces
Ischemia lowers tPA; cytokines raise PAI-1
Fibrin persists beyond about 3 days
Fibroblasts and capillaries invade the fibrin
TGF-beta drives collagen; a fibrous band forms
blocks.caption: The balance between fibrin deposition and fibrinolysis decides whether the surfaces heal free or scar together.

blocks.text: Small bowel obstruction

Adhesions are usually silent until a band kinks mobile small bowel or forms a ring that traps a loop. They cause most small bowel obstructions in adults who have had abdominal surgery, often years later; hernias lead in people who have not. Fixed colon is rarely obstructed by adhesions. Proximal bowel fills with swallowed air and secretions, peristalsis strains against the block (colicky pain, high-pitched bowel sounds), and vomiting, distension, and failure to pass flatus follow. Fluid lost by vomiting and sequestered in the lumen and wall causes hypovolemia, and in proximal obstruction, vomited gastric acid gives hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Radiographs show dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and little colonic gas; adhesions themselves are not visible.

blocks.title: Obstruction to strangulation
steps: Adhesive band kinks or traps a loop
Gas and fluid distend the proximal bowel
Wall pressure rises; venous outflow fails
Wall edema; then arterial inflow fails
Ischemia, necrosis, bacterial translocation
Perforation and peritonitis
blocks.caption: A closed loop cannot decompress in either direction, so it strangulates fastest.

blocks.text: Strangulation changes the picture: pain becomes constant, and fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, raised lactate, and peritoneal signs appear. In the pelvis, adhesions around the fallopian tubes and ovaries cause infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and some adhesions cause chronic pain.

blocks.predict: A woman had an appendectomy 12 years ago. She now has colicky pain, bilious vomiting, distension, and no flatus. What lesion is most likely, and what finding would mean the bowel is dying?
blocks.explain: An adhesive band from the old surgery obstructing the small bowel. Constant pain with fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, raised lactate, or peritoneal signs indicates strangulation.
blocks.check: The small bowel obstruction subsection and the strangulation flow.

integration.text: Physiology and anatomy explain where fluid goes. Starling forces and lymph flow decide whether fluid leaves the sinusoids, and sinusoid histology decides how much protein it carries, which is why SAAG measures pressure while total protein measures permeability. The kidney is normal in cirrhosis; it retains sodium because baroreceptors read a dilated splanchnic bed as underfilling, the same reflex that defends against hemorrhage. Peritoneal anatomy then shapes the clinical signs: somatic parietal nerves explain guarding in secondary peritonitis, and dependent recesses such as the hepatorenal pouch collect fluid and pus.

Microbiology, immunology, and pathology link the three conditions. Translocated aerobic gram-negative rods and weak ascitic opsonization explain monomicrobial SBP, while spilled colonic flora explains polymicrobial secondary peritonitis with anaerobic abscesses. Peritonitis in turn suppresses fibrinolysis and leaves dense adhesions, which later obstruct the bowel. These patterns have limits: secondary peritonitis can arise in cirrhotic ascites, heart failure gives high-SAAG fluid without cirrhosis, and bowel obstruction in a patient without prior surgery points to hernia or tumor rather than adhesions.

summary: Ascites in cirrhosis needs sinusoidal portal hypertension; prehepatic portal vein thrombosis rarely causes it.
Splanchnic nitric oxide vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume and activates RAAS, sympathetic nerves, and nonosmotic ADH, so the kidneys retain sodium and water.
Hypoalbuminemia contributes to ascites, but sinusoidal pressure and renal sodium retention are the main drivers.
A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension; ascitic protein under 2.5 g/dL suggests cirrhosis, and 2.5 g/dL or more suggests heart failure or Budd-Chiari syndrome.
SBP results from bacterial translocation, shunting past Kupffer cells, and poor opsonization in low-protein ascites; it is usually monomicrobial E. coli or Klebsiella.
Ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more diagnose infected ascites; SBP may cause only fever, encephalopathy, or kidney injury.
Secondary peritonitis is polymicrobial with anaerobes, inflames the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, and causes a rigid abdomen and free air if a viscus perforated.
Adhesions form when injury and ischemia lower tPA and raise PAI-1, so fibrin persists and is organized into collagen bands.
Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction after abdominal surgery; a closed loop strangulates fastest.

verify: HVPG thresholds (above 5 mmHg for portal hypertension, 10 mmHg or more as clinically significant) follow current hepatology consensus; confirm they match NABNE expectations.
The SAAG accuracy of about 97% and the 2.5 g/dL total protein cutoff come from the Runyon studies; other sources vary slightly.
The volume needed to detect shifting dullness (about 1,500 mL) varies between sources.
The fluid chemistry criteria for secondary peritonitis (Runyon criteria) and the correction of 1 neutrophil per 250 red cells follow AASLD guidance; confirm they are current.
Estimates of the share of small bowel obstructions caused by adhesions and the share of laparotomy patients who develop adhesions vary widely between sources, so no single figure is given.
